items.text: Many women in the UK are visiting new places called rage room s. In these rooms, people use hammers to break old TVs, plates, and boxes. People go there because they feel very stressed , tired, or sad about life and work. Owners of these rooms say that most of their visitors are women. Doctors say that it is good to let out bad feelings in a safe space. Men can get angry during sports, but women must be quiet and calm. Breaking things makes people feel happy and strong for a short time. But it cannot solve big life problems forever. Difficult words: hammer (a hand tool which we use for breaking things), stressed (worried and upset), owner (a person who has something and it belongs to him or her). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Rage rooms are becoming very popular in the UK, especially for women. In these special rooms, people pay to break things like old TVs, plates, and glasses with big hammers. About 75 percent of the customers are women who are trying to deal with work stress, busy family lives, or deep sadness after losing loved ones. Experts explain that society usually expects women to stay calm, so they don’t have many places to express anger. Smashing things gives people a quick feeling of power and release. On the other hand, doctors say that while rage rooms are fun and help you feel better for a short time, breaking things doesn’t fix big emotional problems forever. Difficult words: rage (uncontrollable anger), sadness (when you are sad), smash (to break something into pieces with great force). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Across the UK, a growing number of people, especially women, are turning to so-called rage rooms to destroy everyday items like flat-screen televisions and crockery with mallets and hammers. Owners report that up to three-quarters of their customers are female. Many use the sessions to cope with everyday stress, child-rearing pressures, or deep emotional trauma such as bereavement . Psychologists note that societal expectations often force women to suppress anger, unlike sports events where men are traditionally permitted to shout freely. Inside a rage room, participants find a safe, controlled environment where they can express frustration without judgment . While smashing objects provides an immediate surge of adrenaline and physical relief, experts caution that it doesn’t serve as a permanent therapeutic cure for long-term psychological problems. Instead, they view it as a helpful short-term release of energy, and advise individuals dealing with deep-seated emotional pain to seek professional long-term support. Difficult words: bereavement (suffering the loss of a loved one through death), suppress (to forcibly hold back, control, or prevent the expression of a feeling), judgment (an opinion or decision formed after thought or legal process). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Many kids love playing with squishy toys. Scientists test some of these toys to see if they are safe. They find that one toy has too much of one chemical. This chemical can hurt children. Also, if squishies stay in a hot car for a long time, they can break. Hot liquid may come out. This can hurt a child’s skin. The store takes the bad toy away. They give money back to parents. Experts tell families to check toy labels and keep the toys away from hot places like cars. Difficult words: squishy (soft, not hard when you touch it), liquid (a substance which flows, like water or gel), label (a piece of paper on a product which gives information about it). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Squishy toys are very popular with children who love to collect and squeeze them. But reports from around the world show that some of these toys may not be safe. A team in Singapore tested 18 squishy toys in a laboratory to check for dangerous chemicals. They found that most toys were fine, but one pink toy had high levels of a chemical called DINP, which is used to make plastic soft. This chemical was higher than local safety limits and can be harmful to children’s health. Tests also showed that if squishies are left in a hot car, they can get very hot, break, and leak dangerous liquid. After finding these results, the store removed the unsafe toy and offered refunds to customers. Difficult words: squishy (a soft toy), safety limit (the maximum amount of a chemical in a product to be still safe), refund (money given back to a customer who returns an unsafe or unwanted product). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Squishy toys have become extremely popular among children, who collect and squeeze them for stress relief. However, international safety concerns have prompted investigations into what these toys contain. Researchers and journalists tested 18 different squishies in Singapore for harmful chemicals like benzene and phthalates that are linked to cancer, hormone disruption , and developmental risks. While no benzene was detected, laboratory testing revealed that several toys contained restricted plasticisers . One pink toy exceeded Singapore’s legal limit by 1.7 times. Experts warn that prolonged heat, such as being left inside a parked car, can cause these toys to soften, leak, or rupture under pressure, and potentially cause skin irritation or burns. Following the findings, the affected retailer pulled the unsafe product from its shelves and offered customers refunds. Authorities advise parents to inspect toy labels carefully, avoid leaving them in direct sunlight, and monitor children during play. Difficult words: phthalate (a chemical additive that makes plastics softer, more flexible, and resilient), hormone disruption (an interference with the hormones, which can affect growth and health), plasticiser (a chemical substance added to materials to increase their softness, flexibility, or stretchiness).
